routes.name: Scratch and Sniff
routes.overview: A mixed outing on a small but adventurous satellite buttress off Mount Francis's NW Ridge, reachable in one day out of Kahiltna's base camp. Cross the schrund and head up a snow ramp angling right for about 300 ft, then belay under a steep corner. Climb the corner (10 m, M6), a chimney that widens and faces left (10 m, M5/6), then a broad chimney through the next rock band. More pitches lead to a traverse leftward across runout snow that is steep, then a runout slab and moderate snow and mixed ground to the summit. Descend by an anchor of nuts and a pin, making three rappels from rock gear, then V-thread rappels.
routes.detailed_rack: Cams to 3 inches, nuts, pins and a few ice screws.

routes.name: Chockstone Route
routes.fa: Wesley Grande, Pete Schoening, and Dick Widrig, May 28, 1950 (peak's first-ascent line, historically also referenced as the Southwest Face Route)
gear: Ice axe and crampons if snow/ice lingers in the gully (common into early summer)
hazards: Much loose rock on the upper pitches, which are often simul-climbed — rockfall risk to your own party and anyone below
Lingering snow/ice in the gully into early summer; a cold, wet crux pitch has been reported to climb closer to 5.8+
routes.overview: Chockstone Route (II+ 5.7) climbs the gully and south face between North and South Early Winters Spire — the original 1950 first-ascent line up the peak. A low-angle slab/layback first pitch (often scrambled or simul-climbed) leads up the gully toward a massive chockstone, bypassed on the left via the 5.7 crux pitch, before chimney systems lead to the summit plateau.
routes.beta: A low-fifth-class slab/layback step leads into gully hiking (often holding snow early season) toward the giant chockstone. A 5.7 pitch bypasses the chockstone on the left via blocky terrain and an exposed lieback, historically protected by old pitons, finishing on a delicate slab with sparse bolt protection. Moderate climbing on golden rock with modern bolts, a rightward traverse, and a final loose gully/chimney lead to the summit plateau.
routes.turnaround: In early season, turn back or reassess if the gully still holds significant snow/ice you're not equipped for (axe/crampons); the crux lieback's old fixed pitons should not be trusted to hold a fall.
routes.rappels: 4 bolted rap stations + 1 tree rappel down a 5.0 slab (60m rope)
routes.face: Southwest side, in the giant chasm between North and South Early Winters Spire
routes.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
routes.comms: No reliable cell coverage at the Blue Lake Trailhead or on the peak; carry a satellite messenger.
routes.descent: Four bolted rappel stations lead down with a single 60m rope; a tree-rappel option down a 5.0 slab also exists near the start of the route.
obj_haz: loose rock, especially in the right-hand gullies near the top
residual snow/ice in the couloir sections early season

waypoints.name: Blue Lake TH
waypoints.note: SR 20 pullout about 1 mi west of Washington Pass.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway just west of Washington Pass. The highway over the pass closes in winter. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required to park.

waypoints.name: Spire col (gully base)
waypoints.note: Base of the gully between North and South Early Winters Spires, below the giant chockstones.
waypoints.directions: Hike the Blue Lake Trail about a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction, then take the climbers' path up through slabs, talus and heather into the basin below the west faces. Head for the foot of the huge cleft that splits North and South Early Winters Spires; this is the west-side gully, not the east-side couloir reached from the highway hairpin.

waypoints.name: Chockstone crux
waypoints.note: 5.7 pitch bypassing the first giant chockstone on the left.
waypoints.directions: Climb a short step of low fifth-class slab and layback moves, then walk up the gully bed, taking cracks and ramps along its left edge, to below the first giant chockstone. Early in the season the gully can hold snow, so carry an axe and crampons.

waypoints.name: North Early Winters Spire
waypoints.directions: Pass the chockstone on the left over blocky ground to an exposed lieback and a delicate slab, then continue on good, bolted rock with a rightward traverse and finish up a loose gully and chimney onto the summit plateau.

timing.recommendedStart: Morning start from the Blue Lake Trailhead, earlier if the gully still holds firm snow

routes.detailed_rack: A single cam rack from 0.5-2in plus a nut set covers the route; bring extra quickdraws for the fixed pins and bolts on the crux and upper pitches.
what_to_bring: Rock shoes plus boots for the snow gully
pro_tips: Take the bolted West Face rappels down instead of the original gully descent - it is faster, cleaner, and safer per repeat parties.
Expect to swap between rock shoes and boots/crampons multiple times if climbing with residual snow in the gully.
routes.watch_out:
Chockstone features create technical and exposed sections
Route-finding through chockstone terrain can be confusing
Weather exposure on exposed terrain
Loose rock hazard throughout approach and mixed sections
Descent route-finding critical in variable terrain
routes.pro_needs: Protection is adequate on the crux 5.7 pitch, but the original fixed pitons here date to the 1940s-50s and should be backed up rather than trusted outright; modern bolts on the upper pitches are more reliable.
routes.best_season: Climbable June through September; parties attempting it soon after snowmelt should carry an ice axe and light crampons for the approach gully, while later-season ascents are drier but the chockstone gully still catches shade and can hold ice longer than the sun-facing routes.
routes.approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft) on SR-20, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, and locate the obvious chasm/gully between North and South Early Winters Spire on the west side of the formations. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base; expect to switch between rock shoes and boots/crampons if snow lingers in the gully.
routes.descent_text: The standard descent uses four bolted rappel stations with a 60m rope, plus one rappel off a tree down the 5.0 slab near the start, located about 30m down and skier's-right of the summit exit. An older/original variant instead makes five rappels straight down the ascent gully, including one free-hanging rappel off the chockstone, through loose and windy terrain; this is considered slower and less pleasant than the bolted West Face option.
routes.bail: Easy to bail from the lower pitches by downclimbing or rappelling the same gully; above the chockstone crux, the bolted West Face rap line offers a quicker, safer retreat than reversing the original gully descent.

pitch_detail.notes: Low fifth-class slab/layback step, often simply scrambled, into gully hiking (can hold snow early season).
Bypasses the huge chockstone on the left via blocky terrain to an exposed lieback, historically protected by old 1940s-50s pitons, finishing on a delicate slab with sparse bolt protection.
Moderate climbing on good rock with modern bolts, a rightward traverse, then a final loose gully/chimney to the summit plateau.

_raw.parking_pass_pickup_locations: National Forest offices, visitor centers, online at recreation.gov

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).

overnight_permit.where: Dispersed camping on National Forest land is free; nearby developed campgrounds charge a site fee and take no reservation.

road.name: Blue Lake Trailhead, SR-20, Washington Pass
road.status: Paved highway parking at the Blue Lake Trailhead; no unpaved road driving required.
road.driveNote: Roughly 3-3.5 hours from Seattle via SR-20 to the Washington Pass area.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 closes seasonally over Washington Pass due to avalanche danger. In 2025-26 it closed Dec 4, 2025; the east side through Washington Pass reopened April 30, 2026, and the whole highway on June 14, 2026 after storm-damage repairs. Dates vary by year.

climate.fall: September-early October often gives stable, cool, dry conditions before winter gating.
climate.spring: SR-20 typically reopens late April-May; the shaded gully holds snow/ice well into early summer.
climate.summer: June-September is the main season, though the gully can still carry snow early on.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed (roughly December-April/May); the peak is effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate: heavy, wet winter snowpack and drier, warmer continental summers.
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass has its own NWAC weather station (5,477 ft); the area falls within NWAC's East Slopes avalanche forecasting and the NWS 'Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest' zone (WAZ522)

emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service (Twisp) provides EMS and high-angle rescue support in the Methow Valley, including Washington Pass, and partners with Okanogan County SAR. There is no cell coverage at the trailhead or on the peak - carry a satellite messenger.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Winthrop, WA
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, 507 Hospital Way, Brewster, WA - 24-hr ER, Level IV trauma
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Okanogan County Sheriff's Office / 911 (dispatches Okanogan County Search and Rescue)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through August, when the gully between the spires has melted out and the loose upper chimneys are dry

May.reason: Once SR 20 reopens in spring the basin and gully are still buried in snow, making this a snow climb rather than a rock route.

July.reason: The gully sheds most of its snow and the chockstone pitch dries, making the route faster, though some snow may linger early.

June.reason: A mixed outing: snow and ice in the gully require axe and crampons plus boot-to-rock-shoe changes, and the crux may be wet.

August.reason: Dry and quick, but loose rock on the upper pitches is exposed and rockfall from parties above is the main hazard.

October.reason: Early snow and ice return to the shaded gully and SR 20 approaches its winter closure, which usually comes in November or December.

September.reason: Still in shape, though the shaded chockstone gully can hold ice after cold nights and days are shorter.

routes.rope_note: 60m rope for the rappel descent: 4 bolted rap stations plus one tree rappel down the 5.0 slab at the very start of the route. Bring an ice axe (and crampons if snow lingers) for the entry gully in early season.
routes.corrections: Mountain Project route page: 'single rack to 2 inches, draws for fixed pins' — a set of nuts and cams 0.5-2in is sufficient; bring extra draws for the fixed gear on the chockstone-bypass pitch.

rappel_detail.pull: 60 m is the stated minimum rope for this line; a 70 m makes every station comfortable.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel, off a tree down a short 5.0 slab from the summit exit area.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree, on the 5.0 slab, about 30m below and skier's-right of the summit exit
rappel_detail.station: The descent does not start where the route tops out. The rappel line begins roughly 30 m down and skier's right of the top-out, reached by walking and downclimbing from the summit exit, so hunt for it rather than rigging off the first thing at the finish.

rappel_detail.notes: First of four bolted single-rope rappels with a 60m rope.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted station (blank section of West Face)
hazards: hanging station - get tethered in before unweighting the rope
rappel_detail.station: Top of the bolted line down the right side of the West Face. The first rappel drops straight down the face to a station described as a hanging belay with no ledge to stand on.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the bolted West Face line.
hazards: the line steps sideways here, so the next anchor is not directly below the rope
rappel_detail.station: Next bolted station down the face; from here the line is described as trending climber's left rather than falling straight down.

rappel_detail.pull: A 70 m rope removes the squeeze entirely.
rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the bolted West Face line.
hazards: rope ends land in the working zone on a 60 m - knot both ends
mixed piton-and-bolt anchor at one station on this line; inspect before loading
rappel_detail.station: Commonly reported as the third rappel of the bolted sequence, and the tight one: on a 60 m rope parties describe reaching down to clip a tether to the anchor and then feeding rope through the device to close the last bit. One station on this line is described as a piton backed by a bolt rather than two bolts.

rappel_detail.pull: Pulls on this line are reported clean and direct, but at least one rappel clears a roof, so expect the ends to hang free of the wall.
rappel_detail.notes: Final bolted rappel reaching the base.
rappel_detail.station: Lowest station; the line puts you back essentially where packs are left at the base. Accounts differ on the bottom of the sequence - some describe the last one or two rappels off tree slings above and below the chimney rather than off bolts.

routes.rappel_count_note: This is the current recommended descent (a tree rap near the top followed by four bolted West Face stations). An older/original variant instead makes 5 rappels straight down the ascent gully - including one free-hanging rappel off the chockstone - through loose, windy terrain, and is less commonly used now that the bolted line exists. Individual rappel lengths are not published; every station is reached on a single 60 m rope.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the chasm between the two spires
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream and a large cairn, then take the climbers' path up through slabs, talus and heather into the basin below the west faces.

The objective from here is the huge cleft that splits the two Early Winters Spires, seen from the west side. Head for its foot. Note this is the west-side gully — the couloir that splits the same two spires on the east side, reached from the highway hairpin, is a different feature and a different route.

Be ready to swap between rock shoes and boots if snow is still lying in the gully.
hazards: snow lingering in the gully early season — axe and crampons
loose rock funnelled down the gully, including from parties above
wind in the gully; it channels weather
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is at the very foot of the enormous chasm dividing North from South Early Winters Spire — it is the biggest single feature on this side of the group and it is unambiguous even in poor visibility, because nothing else on the west faces is a full-height cleft between two summits. The route opens with a short step of low-fifth-class slab and layback moves, and then it is walking up the gully bed; if you are pulling on anything hard in the first rope length you are on one of the face routes to either side, not in the gully. Pitch one takes cracks and ramps along the left edge of the gully rather than the middle. The house-sized chockstone that names the route sits much higher up the same gully, so do not expect to see it from the base as your confirmation.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

routes.name: Colonade

routes.name: Early Winter Couloir
routes.fa: Gary Brill and Lowell Skoog, May 6, 1978
routes.season: A narrow window of a few weeks right after SR-20 reopens each spring, typically April-early May, while snow/ice still fills the couloir
gear: 3-5 pitons and a set of nuts
Ice axe(s) and crampons; optional pickets and ice screws for firm snow/ice sections
Some parties carry rock shoes to swap into for the final rock pitch
hazards: No established rappel stations exist for a descent back down the couloir itself, forcing ad hoc anchors in poor rock -- a fatal accident (May 2025) occurred when an old rusted piton anchor failed, killing 3 climbers; inspect any in-place anchor thoroughly and consider building fresh anchors rather than trusting fixed gear
routes.overview: Early Winter Couloir (III 5.6 AI3 M4+) splits North and South Early Winters Spire and is a mixed snow/ice/rock climb, first done by Gary Brill and Lowell Skoog on 5/6/78. The route passes three large chockstones and a cornice near the top — many parties end up aid-climbing past the cornice — before a final mixed/rock pitch to the summit.
routes.beta: Climbers ascend Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin, traverse north to a 40-degree snow ramp, then climb roughly five pitches of snow/ice/mixed terrain up the couloir (passing three chockstones) to the col between the spires, finishing with a rock pitch to the North Spire's summit. The cornice atop the couloir is frequently the technical and psychological crux, sometimes requiring careful aid, tunneling, or a rock variant to breach.
routes.turnaround: Given the couloir's serious afternoon warming and rockfall/icefall hazard, and the difficulty of a safe descent, parties should be off the technical climbing and descending well before mid-afternoon; a fatal May 2025 accident involved a party still descending after 5:30pm.
routes.rappels: ~4 raps down the bolted West Couloir line (single 60 m rope); no fixed anchors in the couloir itself
routes.face: East-facing gully splitting North and South Early Winters Spire
routes.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
routes.comms: No cell coverage in the couloir or on the peak. In the May 2025 fatal accident, the lone survivor had no signal at the accident site and had to descend and drive roughly 42 miles to Newhalem to call 911 - carry a satellite messenger/InReach.
routes.descent: The standard descent follows the West Couloir on the west side of the peak: bolted anchors lead down with about 4 rappels and some downclimbing to a fixed piton-and-nut anchor at a chockstone, passable with a single rope. Retreating directly back down Early Winter Couloir itself (rather than via the West Couloir) has no established rappel anchors, forcing ad hoc gear anchors in poor rock — the scenario implicated in the May 2025 fatal accident on this route.
obj_haz: avalanche/wet-slide hazard in a narrow, funnel-shaped couloir

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout
waypoints.directions: Park at the hairpin curve on SR-20 roughly a mile southeast of Washington Pass, at about 5,100 ft, directly under the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. This is the east-side start; the Blue Lake Trailhead serves the west side and is the wrong side of the mountain for this route. Access is set entirely by the highway, which is gated over Washington Pass all winter, usually closing in late November or early December and reopening somewhere between mid-April and early May. The couloir is only in condition for a few weeks after that gate opens, so time your drive to the reopening.

waypoints.name: Spire Gully entrance
waypoints.note: Ascend Spire Gully then traverse north to the base of the couloir's snow ramp.

waypoints.name: Summit cornice
waypoints.note: Large cornice guards the top of the couloir; often requires aid/mixed moves and has no fixed rap anchors.

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn, well before first light, from the SR-20 hairpin, to climb on firm snow/ice and be off route and descending well before mid-afternoon

routes.detailed_rack: A 60m rope; cams from 0.2-3in weighted toward the smaller sizes; a small nut set; one or two pickets; and 4-5 pitons (angles/Lost Arrows) for the chockstone and cornice pitches. Ice screws have been reported as largely ineffective given the thin, poor-quality ice typical of this route.
what_to_bring: Boots compatible with crampons and later rock/slab moves
Extra layers for variable snow/ice/rock conditions
pro_tips: Climb it in the narrow window right after SR-20 reopens (late April-early May) for the best snow/ice conditions - it degrades quickly as the season warms.
Start pre-dawn to be off the technical terrain and descending well before afternoon warming.
Always descend via the bolted West Couloir/Chockstone Route rappels, never back down the couloir to the east.
routes.watch_out:
Avalanche and wet-slide path on the approach snow and in the couloir — check the NWAC East Slopes forecast and climb on a cold, firm morning
Thin or absent ice most winters — be ready to dry-tool, condition-dependent climbing
Loose chossy rock on pitch 2 and box gully — protection can be difficult
No established rappel stations for a descent back down the couloir itself (the West Couloir descent is bolted) — inspect any fixed anchors thoroughly, fatal anchor failure recorded (2025)
routes.pro_needs: Protection is thin and marginal through the chockstone and cornice pitches - a mixed rack of small cams, nuts, and pitons is essential; don't rely on ice screws for the ice sections.
routes.best_season: Typically in shape for only a few weeks right after SR-20 reopens for the season each spring (roughly mid/late April into early May), when the snow and ice are still firm; conditions deteriorate quickly as the couloir melts out.
routes.approach: From the Hairpin turn on SR-20 (east side of the Early Winters Spire formation), ascend roughly 1,500 ft of steep approach snow — often waist-deep before it firms up — to reach the couloir's mouth.
routes.descent_text: The standard, safer descent uses the bolted rappel line down the West Couloir, on the Chockstone Route side: about four rappels plus some downclimbing back to the base. Descending the technical couloir back down to the east (the way many parties climb) is documented but dangerous - there are no fixed anchors there, forcing parties to improvise anchors on steep, broken rock, sometimes on old rusted fixed pitons, above a long fall onto talus or snow. A fatal 2025 accident occurred exactly this way.
routes.bail: Bail is difficult once committed above the first chockstone. The safest retreat in deteriorating conditions is to continue to the col and use the bolted West Couloir/Chockstone Route descent rather than improvising rappel anchors on the unequipped east side of the couloir.

pitch_detail.notes: Mixed/snow step past the first chockstone (45-55°) to a tree anchor; includes a short crux of thin ice smeared on the wall.
Snow ramp approach toward the second chockstone.
Crux chockstone pitch - a thin vein of poor-quality ice on the chockstone's right side, slightly overhung to vertical, with delicate frontpointing and tool-hooking.
Good gear leads up to the final chockstone below the cornice.
Breach the cornice via a gap between the couloir wall and the cornice using steep mixed moves and small tool/pick placements; can require aiding, tunneling, or a rock variant.
60+ meters of mixed/slab climbing to the summit plateau; crampons are often removed partway for insecure slab moves in stiff boots.

routes.itinerary: Typical single-day itinerary: pre-dawn start from the car, ~1 hr approach to the couloir base, 5-7 hrs of technical climbing to the col and summit, then descend via the West Couloir/Chockstone bolted rappels (not back down the couloir) in 2-3 hrs, aiming to be off all technical terrain well before dark.

access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.closures: Only accessible once SR-20 reopens for the season (typically late April-May) and before it closes again in winter

road.name: SR-20 hairpin pullout, east of Washington Pass
road.status: Roadside parking at the paved SR-20 hairpin pullout; no unpaved road driving required.
road.driveNote: Roughly 3-3.5 hours from Seattle via SR-20 to the Washington Pass area.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 closes seasonally over Washington Pass due to avalanche danger. In 2025-26 it closed Dec 4, 2025; the east side through Washington Pass reopened April 30, 2026, and the whole highway on June 14, 2026 after storm-damage repairs. Dates vary by year.

climate.fall: The route is rarely climbed in fall due to lack of consolidated snow/ice.
climate.spring: SR-20 typically reopens late April-May, which is also the prime climbing window; avalanche and cornice hazard remain high in this period.
climate.summer: By June-July the couloir has usually melted out into a looser mixed/rock scramble with more rockfall.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed (roughly December-April/May); the couloir is inaccessible from the highway side.
climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate with heavy, wet winter/spring snowpack; the pass corridor is among the highest-avalanche-frequency stretches of highway in the US.
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass has its own NWAC weather station (5,477 ft); the area falls within NWAC's East Slopes avalanche forecasting and the NWS 'Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest' zone (WAZ522) - check the current avalanche/mountain weather forecast before a spring ascent

emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service (Twisp) provides EMS and high-angle rescue support in the Methow Valley, including Washington Pass, and partners with Okanogan County SAR. There is no cell coverage in the couloir or on the peak - carry a satellite messenger. A May 10, 2025 accident here required the sole survivor to drive ~42 miles to Newhalem to reach a phone.

approach_logistics.trailhead: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout (east of Washington Pass)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the hairpin-turn/pond pullout on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass (~5,100 ft), via the cairned climbers' paths

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the summit rock band, starting down the West Couloir/Chockstone side.
hazards: Descending the east-side couloir instead is the documented trap: it holds no fixed anchors, so parties improvise stations on steep broken rock and old rusted pitons. The May 2025 fatal accident on this route happened that way
rappel_detail.station: Off the summit rock band the descent starts down the west/southwest side on the standard summer bolted stations - not back down the couloir you climbed.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down bolted stations, with some downclimbing worked in between rappels.
hazards: Loose rock on the ledges between stations, with the party below you directly in the fall line
rappel_detail.station: Second bolted station on the standard line. Short downclimbs link the stations, so expect to move between anchors on foot rather than rappelling continuously.

rappel_detail.notes: Passes the steepest, most broken sections of the West Couloir face.
hazards: Route-finding, not steepness, is the difficulty here: several rappel lines exist on this face and only this one leads to the chockstone exit
rappel_detail.station: The third rappel is the one that lands you in the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire. That notch is the aiming point for the whole upper sequence - if you are not heading toward it you are on the wrong line.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull clear of the chockstone's underside - the strands hang free past it and a knot pulled up against the block is awkward to reach from below.
rappel_detail.notes: Short (~50 ft) free rappel past the 'giant chockstone' to reach lower-angle terrain near the base; a single 60m rope is sufficient for the whole descent.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed piton-and-nut anchor in the wall beside the chockstone
hazards: Largely free-hanging as you clear the chockstone, with no wall contact to steady you or to fend off a spin
The exit below traverses under South Early Winters Spire's southwest rib into Spire Gully, which postholes badly in soft snow
rappel_detail.station: From the notch, the final rappel takes you past the large chockstone in the West Couloir. The anchor is NOT on the chockstone itself - it is a fixed piton-and-nut station in the skier's-right wall, and a single rope gets you down past the blockage.

routes.rappel_count_note: Four rappels plus downclimbing, on a single 60 m rope, using the standard summer bolted stations down the west side to the North/South Early Winters Spire notch, then the piton-and-nut anchor in the skier's-right wall to get past the West Couloir chockstone. The competing figure of about six belongs to a different line: a newer, fully bolted rappel route down the right side of the West Face, roughly six stations spaced about 100 ft (30 m) apart. That line does not include the chockstone rappel; a 60 m rope only just works on it, and on its third station you have to reach down to clip in before letting the rope run through, so knot the ends. Do not mix stations between the two lines.

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (snow)
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the hairpin curve on SR-20 roughly a mile southeast of Washington Pass, directly under the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. This is the east-side approach; the Blue Lake Trailhead serves the west side and is the wrong side of the mountain for this route.

From the pullout, go straight up Spire Gully on snow. Reports put it at around 1,500 feet of steep snow to the start of the technical ground, and in April that snow can be unconsolidated enough to posthole to the waist — one party described slogging in to the thigh and beyond, while a party on firmer May snow was at the base in under an hour from the car. Time it for a cold night and an early start.

The window is narrow and it is set by the highway. SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated all winter, usually closing late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May, and this route is only in condition for a few weeks after that gate opens.
approach_variants.season: A few weeks right after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr to early May
hazards: 1,500 ft of steep snow with avalanche and wet-slide potential on a sun-affected aspect
deep unconsolidated snow early in the window
no fixed anchors in the couloir — a party that retreats down it is improvising anchors on steep broken rock, and a fatal accident occurred this way in 2025
cornice at the top of the couloir
route only exists once SR-20 reopens, and closes out within weeks
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir is the obvious gash splitting the two spires as seen from the highway — you can pick it out from the hairpin before you start walking, which is the best moment to fix it in your mind if cloud is forecast. From the top of Spire Gully do not continue straight up into the cleft; traverse north to gain a ramp of snow lying at about 40 degrees, and the technical climbing starts from the top of that ramp. The ramp is the handrail: a distinctly moderate-angled snow feature leading leftward into the base of the steeper couloir. Parties that push straight into the cleft from the gully below the ramp are starting too low.

routes.name: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack Route)
routes.fa: Paul Boving and Steve Pollack, September 25, 1976
gear: Extra-long slings/alpine draws for the leftward-traversing pitches
60-70m rope (needed if descending via the bolted West Face rappel line)
hazards: The route includes wide flake and offwidth pitches that require big gear; running low on large cams is a real risk.
Long, sometimes traversing pitches create rope drag that must be managed with long runners.

The Early Winters Spires are a serious alpine setting: on May 10, 2025, three climbers died and a fourth was seriously injured when a single old, rusted piton anchor pulled out while multiple people were clipped to it and rappelling in the Early Winter Couloir, the gully separating North and South Early Winters Spire (a different line than this route's own NW Corner descent gully). It's a hard reminder never to trust an old fixed pin without backup and never to load one anchor point with an entire party.
routes.overview: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack), 5.9+ III, is the classic moderate outing on North Early Winters Spire, the northern/lower of the two Early Winters Spires in the Liberty Bell Group at Washington Pass. First climbed by Paul Boving and Steve Pollack on September 25, 1976, it follows a corner system, the well-known 'Zig-Zag Flakes' pitch, and a burly offwidth up the peak's northwest aspect in 4-5 pitches (roughly 500 ft of climbing), finishing with a 4th-class traverse around a roof to the summit. It's one of the most popular moderate alpine rock routes at Washington Pass alongside the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell and the South Arete on South Early Winters Spire.
routes.beta: The Northwest Corner is a well-established four-to-five pitch route that ascends the natural corner system on the northwest aspect of North Early Winters Spire. This is one of the most popular routes on the peak, known for reliable rock quality and manageable protection requirements. The route follows a clear line with sustained climbing throughout.
routes.turnaround: Top out before afternoon thunderstorms; the spire summit is highly exposed.
routes.rappels: Two lines: the bolted West Face (six bolted stations), all single-rope on a 60 m rope that just barely reaches - a 70 m is the comfortable choice - or the classic line (3 single-rope raps to the notch, then a largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past the chockstone, then a short tree rap)
routes.permit: No climbing permit required; a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or day-use fee (Digital Day Pass / Scan & Pay) is needed for trailhead parking.
routes.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable on the route and summit; Verizon generally provides the best coverage among carriers. Coverage at the trailhead is variable. Satellite communication device (satellite phone or personal locator beacon) recommended for emergencies in this remote alpine location.
routes.descent: Follow the standard spire descent off the back side.
obj_haz: loose rock in trees on P1-P2

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 30 miles, over Washington Pass, to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway about a mile west of the pass, at roughly 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or day-use fee is required to park. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, so there is no drive-up access until it reopens in spring.

waypoints.name: North Early Winters Spire
waypoints.directions: Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the signed climbing-access junction just past a small stream (the last water), then take the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces and traverse north along the base to a corner and crack leading to a treed ledge. Five pitches of 5.8-5.9 corners, wide cracks and an offwidth finish left around a roof to the summit.

routes.detailed_rack: Doubles 0.75"-3" (BD sizes 2-4), a single 4" (#5) piece, and singles from fingers to 1" cover the lower corner pitches; the P4 offwidth wants the #4-5 pieces though the climbing is more secure than it looks via face-smears/arm-bars even where gear is sparse. Carry several extra-long slings for P2, P3, and the P5 roof traverse to control rope drag. A 60m rope is the minimum for the bolted West Face rappel descent.
pro_tips: Carry a few extra long slings to extend belays on P2, P3, and the P5 roof traverse and cut rope drag
If descending the classic gully, inspect any fixed piton before weighting it and back it up with your own gear
Prefer the newer 6-station bolted rappel line down the West Face when rope length and conditions allow — cleaner and faster than the loose gully
A 70m rope is more comfortable than 60m if you plan to descend via the bolted rap line
On P2, stay left/on-line off the belay ledge — parties have accidentally wandered right onto the adjacent West Face route here.
watch_out: Inspect any fixed piton before weighting it on the descent and back it up with your own gear (cam, picket, or nut) — see the 2025 anchor-failure fatality on this peak's east-side gully
Stay left on P2 to avoid drifting onto the neighboring West Face route
P4's offwidth and P5's slab both get noticeably harder/wetter in early season or after rain given the NW aspect
Start early to be off the summit before typical PNW afternoon thunderstorm buildup
routes.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack to #4 Camalot with doubles in the 2-4" range, plus a single #5; a 60m (70m more comfortable) rope if descending via the bolted rappel line.
routes.best_season: Prime conditions are typically August into September once the north-facing rock has dried out; the route can still hold snow and wet rock into late June/early July given its NW aspect, especially after a big winter. Check NWAC's Washington Pass zone and recent trip reports for approach/gully snow before an early-season attempt.
routes.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of Hwy 20 (elev. ~5,400 ft), about one mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook and roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop. Follow the well-graded Blue Lake Trail southwest through subalpine forest. At about 1.4-1.5 miles, watch for a signed junction: the main trail continues straight toward Blue Lake, while a climber's path splits left/south, signed for "Liberty Bell Trail #727 – Climbing Access," reached just past a small stream/meadow that is the last reliable water source before the basin. Take the climber's trail, which switchbacks up through slabs, talus, and heather meadows into the Liberty Bell/Early Winters basin beneath the west faces of the spire group — roughly another 0.5 mile and 1,000-1,300 ft of gain, putting total approach distance at about 2 miles with 1,300-1,600 ft of gain from the car (most parties report 1-2 hours). From the upper basin, continue scrambling/traversing north along the base of North Early Winters Spire's west side to a distinctive corner/crack system that leads to a tree-covered ledge — the shared start for the Northwest Corner and West Face. Hazards: lingering snow and occasional avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully well into June (many early-season parties boot or ski the lower approach), talus and slab sections with some route-finding among braided climbers' paths, and no dependable water once past the stream near the Liberty Bell Trail junction, so fill up there.
routes.descent_text:
Two established ways off the summit; both are widely used and either works, but they return you to different spots relative to a gear stash at the base.

Bolted West Face rappel line (most direct back to packs at the base of NW Corner/West Face): from the summit, downclimb/walk skier's-left to the top of a clean, purpose-bolted rappel line down the right side of the West Face. Six bolted (2-bolt) rappel stations in a nearly direct line bring you back down to essentially the same spot where you left your pack at the base of the route. Pulls are reported as clean and the line is efficient — regulars find it a breeze. A single 60m rope is just barely sufficient (one station, reportedly the 3rd rappel, is tight enough that you may need to reach down to clip your PAS/daisy to the anchor and feed rope through your device to reach it); a 70m rope removes that squeeze and is the more comfortable choice. No natural anchors needed on this line — it's fully bolted.

Classic notch/chockstone descent (South/Southwest Gully): downclimb and rappel the south side into the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then continue down the Southwest Gully (the South Early Winter Spire "Chockstone Route" descent). This runs three single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the notch/gully (which often holds snow even in summer), followed by one spectacular, largely free-hanging double-rope rappel down and past a huge chockstone (~50 ft of air), then a final short rappel (~30 ft, off a tree anchor) or downclimb/scramble to reach the base. Total is about 4-5 rappels on this line. Anchors are natural/fixed slings around the chockstone and trees rather than bolts — inspect webbing before trusting it. Summit-to-base time on this descent is typically around 1.5-2 hours. This option is the standard descent if you climbed a route on the south/southwest side, or as a backup if the West Face bolt line is congested or iced.
routes.bail: Belay ledges allow retreat, but the wide pitches make lowering/rappelling awkward; plan gear accordingly.

pitch_detail.notes: 45m crack/corner topped by a short, poorly protected chimney section; easy climbing gains a broad, tree-covered ledge used as the first belay.
50m up and left, weaving through trees (and often lingering snow patches) and a corner to reach a second belay ledge; sustained but moderate climbing.
30m up a left-leading flake and wide crack requiring big cams (bring the #4-#5!); committing 5.9 liebacks lead to a belay slung around a small rock pillar.
25m of surprisingly secure offwidth: smear the face while arm-barring the crack for balance. Widely cited as the burly technical crux, ending at a sloping ledge below a roof.
30m traverse left around the roof (watch rope drag), then easing cracks lead directly to the summit; low 4th class scrambling to finish.

itinerary.cal: Route is dry-season rock only; Hwy 20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated by snow in winter and typically doesn't open until mid/late spring, so plan for a June-September window.

days.note: This is a standard single-day alpine rock outing out of Washington Pass, not an overnight trip. Parties hike the Blue Lake Trail and climber's path into the basin below the Liberty Bell group, scramble to the base, climb 4-5 pitches of sustained 5.8-5.9 up the corner/dihedral system, then descend via a bolted rappel line straight back to the packs.
days.title: Car-to-car: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack)

schedule.label: Leave Blue Lake trailhead
schedule.detail: Early start is typical to beat afternoon thunderstorms and other parties to the route.

schedule.label: Reach base of route
schedule.detail: ~1.5 mi on the Blue Lake Trail, then the well-worn climber's trail into the basin and a short scramble to the start.

schedule.label: Start climbing (P1, 5.8 corner)
schedule.detail: 5 pitches, mostly sustained 5.9 with a burly 3-4" crack higher up; some parties link to 4 pitches.

schedule.label: Top out
schedule.detail: ~3.5 hrs of climbing for a fit, competent party.

schedule.label: Begin bolted rappels down the West Face
schedule.detail: About six single-rope rappels on bolts land back at the packs; a 70m rope is more comfortable than a 60m.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Retrace the climber's trail and Blue Lake Trail to the car.

days.objective: Climb the 5-pitch NW Corner and be back at the car same day

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day car-to-car: roughly 7-8 hours round trip, about 2,600 ft of total gain over ~5.2 miles, no camping involved.

climate.fall: Good into September if the rock has fully dried.
climate.spring: Can still hold snow on the approach into June; some parties ski the approach in early season.
climate.summer: Best window, though still slower to dry after rain than south/west aspects.
climate.typical: Dry, sunny alpine summers are typical July-September with cool nights; the NW-facing rock on this route holds snow and stays damp later into the season than south-facing Washington Pass routes nearby.

bySeason.fall: Can be dry and cool with larch color by late Sept-Oct, but shortening days and early-season snow are a risk.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in July-August, the peak of the Washington Pass rock season
crowds.estimatePerSeason: No published route-specific count found; estimated roughly 20-40 parties per season given Washington Pass is one of the most-visited North Cascades rock climbing areas, tempered by the route's offwidth pitch and big-gear requirement which filter out less experienced/prepared parties compared to easier Washington Pass classics

fitnessSpec.hiking: Moderate approach hike/scramble from the Blue Lake trailhead area on Hwy 20, roughly 2-3 miles with meaningful elevation gain on climber's-trail terrain
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light single-day rack + rope + layers (roughly 15-25 lb); no glacier or overnight gear needed

partner_requirements.approachTime: Roughly 1.5-2.5 hours from the highway pullout to the base of the route
requiredSkills: offwidth/wide-crack technique (or willingness to grovel through the wide Pitch 4 section) plus enough big cams to protect it
multi-pitch rope management on long, traversing pitches to avoid drag
building and, critically, inspecting/backing up rappel anchors for the descent
basic alpine route-finding on an unmarked, featured granite face
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid alpine rock leader with prior multi-pitch trad experience; comfortable leading sustained 5.9/5.9+ granite well above gear and managing rope drag on traversing pitches. Not a suitable first alpine rock route.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June through September, with July-August offering the most consistently dry rock and stable weather

July.reason: Prime Washington Pass season - warm, generally dry granite, and the most reliable stretch of stable high-pressure weather

June.reason: Only the tail end of June is typically in season; earlier in the month lingering snow patches on the approach and wet/cold rock are common before the route reliably comes into condition

August.reason: Continues to be prime season with dry rock, though this is also peak crowd season and can bring hot easterly heat waves

September.reason: Still climbable with cooling, often stable weather, but shorter daylight and an increasing chance of an early-season storm system moving in toward month's end

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades summer alpine pattern - clear, cool mornings with rock that can be slow to dry after a wet spell; the east-side Washington Pass microclimate is drier and can run hot in July-August compared to the west slopes
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/build-ups are the main risk, most common in July and August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Serious, sustained multi-pitch alpine exposure on 5.9+ terrain with committing traversing sections that create rope drag if not managed. The highest-consequence part of the route is the rappel descent, not the climbing itself: a May 2025 accident in which a rappel anchor failed on the North Spire and killed three climbers is a direct reminder to inspect and back up all rappel anchors rather than trusting fixed tat.

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer rock route; the approach falls within NWAC's East Slopes North forecast zone in winter/spring, but that has no bearing on the Late June-September climbing window

gaps: Published elevation is disputed between sources (roughly 7,760-7,789 ft) and not independently resolved here

Pitch count is reported as 4 or 5 depending on how a given party links pitches
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR-20 (~1 mile west of Washington Pass, 5,400 ft), via the Blue Lake Trail to the climbers' path

rappel_detail.notes: First of three single-rope rappels down the south side toward the notch. Plan on near the full reach of a doubled 60 m rope.
hazards: committing to the wrong descent is the easy mistake here - the bolted West Face rappels start well away from this line
rappel_detail.station: This is the classic line, not the bolted West Face one, and the two leave the summit from different places. Scramble down south and west of the summit, then down and skier's left toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire; the first fixed station is on that side.

rappel_detail.notes: Second single-rope rappel continuing toward the notch/gully.
Third single-rope rappel reaching the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.
hazards: the notch is often still snow-covered in summer - expect a wet or snowy stance and possibly a footwear change at the anchor
rappel_detail.station: This rappel lands in the notch and Southwest Couloir between North and South Early Winters Spire.

rappel_detail.pull: Described as a double-rope rappel; check the pull before the second climber commits, since there is no way back up to the anchor once you are hanging free.
rappel_detail.notes: Largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past a huge chockstone (~50 ft/15m of air). Plan on a typical double-rope pitch.
hazards: free-hanging and spinning below the chockstone
the anchor is webbing around a natural feature rather than hardware - inspect it and replace or back it up
rappel_detail.station: Fixed slings on the large chockstone blocking the couloir. The rappel goes off and past the chockstone and is largely free-hanging, about 50 ft of air.

rappel_detail.notes: Final short (~30 ft) rappel, or downclimb/scramble alternative, reaching the base of the Southwest Gully.
rappel_detail.station: Short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree at the bottom of the couloir; scrambling and downclimbing is the accepted alternative if the tree or its slings look poor.

routes.rappel_count_note: Two established descents. The bolted West Face line is six bolted single-rope stations; a 60 m rope only just reaches and a 70 m is the comfortable choice. The classic line is three single-rope rappels to the notch, a free-hanging double-rope rappel past the chockstone, then a short tree rappel or a downclimb to the ground; the table below lists the classic line.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then north along the base of the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Nearly all the routes on North Early Winters Spire are on its west side, so the Blue Lake Trailhead is the right side of the mountain to start from — the hairpin pullout on the east serves the East Buttress and couloir lines, not this one.

From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail for roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction, which sits just past a small stream and is marked with a large cairn. That stream is your last reliable water.

Trail #727 switchbacks up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces. Approach as if for South Early Winters Spire and then traverse left (north) along the base of the formations, scrambling, until you are under North Early Winters Spire. Most parties report one to two hours from the car.
hazards: lingering snow and avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully into June
braided climbers' paths through the upper talus make it easy to drift onto the wrong formation
no water past the stream at the Trail #727 junction
poorly protected chimney section low on the first pitch
approach_variants.baseFinding: Keep traversing north along the base. The Northwest Corner begins at a distinct corner-and-crack system whose first pitch — around 45 metres of 5.8, including a short chimney section with sparse gear — runs up to a broad ledge covered in trees. That treed ledge is the landmark: it is visible from below and from across the basin, it is the top of pitch one, and the route continues up and left off its left-hand edge. If you are under blank slab with no corner leading to a treed ledge, you have not gone far enough north yet. The corner start is shared with the West Face route, so being at the right corner puts you at the right place for either — the two diverge above the ledge, not below it.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

areas.name: North Early Winters Spire
areas.blurb: North Early Winters Spire is a granite spire in the Liberty Bell Group at Washington Pass on the North Cascades Highway (SR-20), directly above the Blue Lake basin. It is the northern/lower of the two Early Winters Spires, separated from South Early Winters Spire by a deep notch (Early Winter Couloir). Published elevations vary by source (roughly 7,760-7,789 ft); prominence is commonly listed around 220 ft.
